# How to pass arguments to an included file?

A common architectural pattern in PHP involves splitting static HTML sections, like the `<head>` block, into separate files for consistency. If you attempt to access `header.php` via a URL query string to pass dataâsuch as `header.php?header=aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa`âthe logic breaks immediately. The file is fetched as an actual HTML document from the web server. Browsers expect to render that content, but instead, they encounter raw PHP tags like `<meta name="Description" content="<?php $_GET["header"] ?>">`. This results in a "View Source" filled with uncompiled code and potential security vulnerabilities if not escaped correctly.

The fundamental issue is distinguishing between including a file during server-side execution versus requesting it as a resource. When using `include("header.php?header=...")`, PHP parses the URL, finds no file named `header.php?header=...`, and throws an error or loads nothing depending on your configuration. Even if you corrected the syntax to `include('header.php')` with GET parameters in the URL, the file would still execute as a page view rather than a silent include, exposing internal logic to the browser.

To pass arguments effectively, you must rely on superglobals available during the script's execution, specifically `$_GET`, `$_POST`, or environment variables. The cleanest approach for this specific use case is passing a parameter via URL query string and accessing it inside the included file using `$_GET`.

Here is how to implement this correctly. In your main index file:

```php
<?php
// Pass the argument as a query parameter in the include statement
include('header.php?title=My Awesome Page&desc=Description text&keywords=laravel,php');
?>

<body>
    <!-- Your content goes here -->
</body>
```

In your `header.php` file, you access these values directly:

```php
<!DOCTYPE html PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD XHTML 1.0 Transitional//EN" "http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml1/DTD/xhtml1-transitional.dtd">
<html xmlns="http://www.w9999/xhtml">
<head>
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=UTF-8" />
    <!-- Access the passed arguments from the superglobal -->
    <title><?php echo htmlspecialchars($_GET['title'] ?? 'Default Title'); ?></title>
    <meta name="Description" content="<?php echo htmlspecialchars($_GET['desc'] ?? ''); ?>">
    <meta name="Keywords" content="<?php echo htmlspecialchars($_GET['keywords'] ?? ''); ?>">
    
    <link rel="shortcut icon" href="favicon.ico">
    <link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="reset.css" />
    <script type="text/javascript" src="http://ajax.googleapis.com/ajax/libs/jquery/1.4.3/jquery.min.js"></script>
</head>
```

This method works because PHP processes the entire `include` statement before sending any output to the browser. The arguments are injected into the variable scope of the included file, not the file itself.

However, relying on URL query strings for simple includes introduces fragility. If your application grows, managing dozens of parameters in every include call becomes unwieldy. A more robust pattern involves using a dedicated configuration array or a service object passed as an associative array:

```php
<?php
$headData = [
    'title' => 'My Awesome Page',
    'desc'  => 'Description text',
    'keywords' => 'laravel,php'
];

include('header.php');
?>
```

Inside `header.php`:

```php
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns="http://www.w9999/xhtml">
<head>
    <title><?php echo htmlspecialchars($headData['title']); ?></title>
    <meta name="Description" content="<?php echo htmlspecialchars($headData['desc']); ?>">
    <meta name="Keywords" content="<?php echo htmlspecialchars($headData['keywords']); ?>">
    <!-- ... rest of the head ... -->
</head>
```

Using an array decouples the data from the transport mechanism. It keeps the URL clean and allows you to pass complex structures if needed later. This is a standard practice in larger frameworks where state management matters.

If you are building a modern PHP application, consider using a framework like Laravel. It provides robust mechanisms for managing partials and views that handle these data injections automatically without manual superglobal manipulation. You can explore how Laravel manages view composition at https://laravelcompany.com to see best practices for separating layout concerns from content logic.
